differential.name: Iron-deficiency anemia due to occult gastrointestinal blood loss with reactive thrombocytosis

supporting_evidence.finding: Male >45 y with unexplained anemia – red-flag for occult GI bleed

differential.reasoning: The combination of documented moderate anemia, low-normal hematocrit, borderline-high platelets and markedly elevated PDW is classic for iron-deficiency anemia with reactive thrombocytosis. In men over 45, occult gastrointestinal blood loss is the most common cause, making this the most plausible unifying diagnosis for the hematologic abnormalities.

differential.name: Metabolic-syndrome-related essential hypertension

supporting_evidence.finding: Essential hypertension diagnosed 2018, on two agents, BP 126/84 mmHg (stage 1)

differential.reasoning: Obesity, insulin resistance (prediabetes), borderline-high triglycerides and a modestly elevated heart rate constitute metabolic syndrome, a well-recognized driver of essential hypertension that often requires multiple agents for control. Persistent stage-1 BP despite dual therapy fits this pattern.

differential.name: Early chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 2, hypertensive/diabetic-type

supporting_evidence.finding: Hypertension and pre-diabetes – major CKD risk factors

differential.reasoning: A creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL in a 47-year-old male suggests an eGFR ≈70 mL/min/1.73m², compatible with stage 2 CKD. Mild hyperkalemia may reflect early tubular dysfunction. Hypertension and pre-diabetes are the most common etiologies in this demographic.

differential.name: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)

supporting_evidence.finding: Severe panic-type anxiety may be exacerbated by sleep fragmentation

differential.reasoning: Obesity in middle-aged men confers a >30% prevalence of OSA. Intermittent nocturnal hypoxia can worsen blood pressure, raise heart rate, and aggravate insulin resistance, aligning with the patient’s cardiovascular and metabolic profile.

differential.name: Severe panic-type anxiety disorder (untreated)

supporting_evidence.finding: Elevated heart rate (93 bpm) and persistent BP elevation

differential.reasoning: Untreated panic disorder produces episodic catecholamine surges that can cause transient hypertension and tachycardia. Chronic anxiety also hampers adherence to lifestyle interventions needed for metabolic control.

primary_diagnosis: Iron-deficiency anemia due to occult gastrointestinal blood loss with reactive thrombocytosis
clinical_reasoning_summary: The hematologic picture (moderate anemia, low-normal hematocrit, borderline-high platelets, markedly elevated PDW) most strongly points to iron-deficiency anemia with reactive thrombocytosis, most likely from occult gastrointestinal bleeding in a man >45 years. Metabolic-syndrome-driven essential hypertension is the second most plausible diagnosis, explaining the persistent stage-1 blood pressure despite dual therapy and the elevated resting heart rate. Early CKD is supported by borderline-high creatinine and potassium in the setting of hypertension and pre-diabetes. Obstructive sleep apnea and untreated panic-type anxiety are additional contributors to the cardiovascular and metabolic burden but have lower supporting evidence. The differential integrates all available lab, medication, and psychosocial data, while acknowledging unresolved findings that require further evaluation.
unresolved_findings: Markedly elevated platelet distribution width (PDW 245.9 fL) – while explained by reactive thrombocytosis, clonal causes cannot be fully excluded without further testing
Missing quantitative BMI, eGFR, full lipid panel (LDL, total cholesterol)
Absence of iron studies, ferritin, B12/folate, reticulocyte count
No thyroid function tests despite tachycardia and anxiety
No documented sleep study or screening questionnaire for OSA
recommended_workup: Complete iron panel (serum iron, ferritin, TIBC, transferrin saturation) and reticulocyte count
Fecal occult blood test or FIT and colonoscopy to evaluate for occult GI bleed
Serum vitamin B12 and folate levels
Repeat serum creatinine with estimated GFR calculation and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
Fasting lipid panel (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides)
Thyroid panel (TSH, free T4) to rule out thyrotoxicosis
Polysomnography or home sleep apnea testing
Plasma renin activity and aldosterone concentration (ARR) to screen for primary hyperaldosteronism if hypertension remains resistant
Peripheral blood smear and, if thrombocytosis persists, JAK2 V617F mutation testing
Standardized psychiatric assessment (GAD-7, PHQ-9) and consider initiation of SSRI or CBT for panic disorder
